prompt: `ana` was made with `Object.create(reader)` and has no `greet`. Why does `ana.greet()` work?
hint: Where does a lookup go when the object lacks the property?

choices.why: `Object.hasOwn(ana, "greet")` was `false`.
Right. `reader` is `ana`'s prototype.

choices.text: Every object has a `greet` method built in
choices.why: No built-in object has one.
It was written inside `reader`.

prompt: Inside `greet`, found on `reader` but called as `ana.greet()`, what is `this`?

choices.why: Where it was found does not matter; how it was called does.
Right: the object before the dot. It printed `hello from ana`.
Inherited methods get `this` like any other.
That is a plain call in sloppy mode.

prompt: `ana.shelves.push("Romance")` changed what `bia.shelves` shows, but `bia.shelves = ["Poetry"]` did not change `ana`'s. Why the difference?
hint: One is a read, one is a write.

choices.text: `push` copies the array to every object that shares it
choices.why: There is one array, on the prototype.
Order of creation does not matter.

choices.text: Lookups go up the chain; an assignment goes on `bia`
choices.why: Right. That is why prototypes hold methods, not data.

choices.text: Arrays on prototypes cannot be reassigned
choices.why: The assignment worked; it went on `bia`.

prompt: Giving an object its own property with the same name as one on its prototype is said to ___ the inherited one.
hint: The word lesson 3 used for names.

prompt: What is at the end of every prototype chain?

choices.why: Right. The walk stops there.
It is the last object, and its own prototype is `null`.
That is what a failed lookup returns, not the end of the chain.
That is one step in an array's chain.

prompt: Put the prototype chain of `["Iracema"]` in order, starting from the array.
trap: `Object.prototype` is the last object, not the end: its own prototype is `null`.

prompt: `list.map === Array.prototype.map` printed `true`. What does that show?

choices.text: Each array gets its own copy, which happens to be equal
choices.why: Two functions are `===` only if they are one function.
Nothing was copied; the array links to it.

choices.text: There is one `map`, found by walking up one step
choices.why: Right.
It lives on `Array.prototype`.

prompt: What is the difference between `Book.prototype` and `Object.getPrototypeOf(Book)`?
hint: One is an ordinary property of the function.

choices.text: None: they are two ways to read the same link
choices.why: That confusion is the one the section warns about.

choices.text: The first becomes the prototype of Book's instances; the second is Book's own prototype
choices.why: Right. `Book` is a function, and its prototype is `Function.prototype`.

choices.text: `Book.prototype` is the old name and `getPrototypeOf` the new one
choices.why: The old name for the link is `__proto__`.

choices.text: The first is `null` until an instance is created
choices.why: It exists as soon as the function does.

prompt: Put the four steps of `new Book("Iracema", 1865)` in order.
hint: The object exists before the function runs.
items: Call `Book` with `this` as the new object
trap: The prototype is linked before `Book` runs, so methods are already reachable inside the constructor.

prompt: Why did `Object.keys(b)` list only `title` and `year`, not `describe`?

choices.why: It lists any own property, functions included.
Right, shared by every book.
It was added before, and placement is what matters.

choices.text: `Object.keys` sorts functions to the end and cuts them
choices.why: It does not sort or cut.

prompt: `Book("Dom Casmurro", 1899)`, without `new`, threw in strict mode. What would it have done without strict mode?
hint: In a plain sloppy call, `this` is the global object.

choices.why: Without `new` nothing creates an object.
`this` would not be `undefined`, so nothing would throw.
Right, which is worse than the error.
The function returns nothing.

prompt: What did `typeof Book` print for the class `Book`?
hint: A class is built on what the last section used.

choices.why: `typeof` has no such answer.
Instances are objects; the class is something else.
Right. A class is a constructor function underneath.
That is not a `typeof` answer.

prompt: Where does a method written in a class body, such as `describe()`, end up?

choices.text: On every instance, copied by the constructor
choices.why: The instance's keys were only `title` and `year`.
Right, shared by all books.
That is where `static` methods go.
Private fields start with `#`.

prompt: Match each piece of the `Book` class with what it is.
hint: Look at the notes beside the example.

pairs.right: Shared by every book through the prototype

prompt: `Book("Iracema")` with a class threw `Class constructor Book cannot be invoked without 'new'`. What does that guarantee over the old constructor function?
hint: Compare with the last section's error.

choices.text: A clear refusal at the call, never globals
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: That the class can be called both ways
choices.why: It refused the call without `new`.

choices.text: That the instance is created even without `new`
choices.why: Nothing was created.
The call did not run at all.

prompt: Why is an `EBook` also `instanceof Book`?

choices.why: Nothing is copied; the chain is linked.

choices.text: Every class is an instance of every other
choices.why: `instanceof` checks a specific chain.
Right. `instanceof` walks that chain.

choices.text: `super()` makes it a Book and then an EBook
choices.why: It is one object with one chain.

prompt: What does `super.describe()` do inside `EBook`'s `describe`?

choices.why: That would never end; `super` skips past `EBook`.
Right, and `EBook` adds the size to it.
That is `super(…)` with no method name.
It calls the parent's `describe`.

prompt: Why did `no-super.js` fail?

choices.why: It had one.

choices.text: `extends` cannot be used with a constructor
choices.why: It can; the order inside was wrong.

choices.text: `super` must be the last line of the constructor
choices.why: It must come before any use of `this`, not last.
Right. The object does not exist until the parent's constructor has run.

prompt: Defining a method on a subclass with the same name as one on its parent is called ___ it.
hint: The lookup finds the subclass's first.

prompt: Which of these shows `#balanceCents` from outside the class?

choices.why: It printed `[ 'owner' ]`.
It printed only the owner.
It printed `Account { owner: 'ana' }`.

choices.text: None of them; only code in the class reaches it
choices.why: Right. The getter is the class's way to share it.

prompt: `acc.#balanceCents` written outside the class: when is the problem found?

choices.text: When the line runs, as a `TypeError`
choices.why: The error was a `SyntaxError`.

choices.text: Before anything runs, as the file is read
choices.why: Right. The program did not start.
That is what a missing ordinary property does.
It is a syntax error in any mode.

prompt: `acc.balance = 5` left the balance at 1990, with no error. Why?
hint: `balance` has a getter and nothing else.

choices.text: The assignment created a private field `#balance`
choices.why: Private fields can only be declared in the class body.

choices.text: Five cents is below the minimum deposit
choices.why: The assignment never reached `deposit`.

choices.text: A getter with no setter takes no assignment, and a sloppy file stays silent
choices.why: Right. Lesson 20 shows it throwing in strict mode.
Nothing was frozen.

prompt: `increment = () => {…}` as a class field kept `this` when called as `press()`. What is the cost the section names?

choices.why: An arrow field in the class body can.

choices.text: It runs more slowly than a method
choices.why: The section names memory, not speed.

choices.text: One copy per instance, not one shared
choices.why: Right. The comparison printed `false`.

choices.text: It cannot be removed as a listener
choices.why: One stable reference per object makes removal easy.

prompt: A colleague says "classes in JavaScript replaced prototypes". What would you correct?

choices.text: Nothing: classes do not use prototypes
choices.why: A class's methods sit on its `prototype`.

choices.text: Classes are syntax over the same prototype chain
choices.why: Right. A class is a function, and its methods live on its prototype.

choices.text: Prototypes are only used by arrays now
choices.why: Every object has a prototype or `null`.

choices.text: Classes copy their methods into each instance instead
choices.why: `Object.keys` showed they do not.
